conceptTag: Take an app to a new country
readerTitle: Your app can launch anywhere. Your business can't.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (가사 청소 예약 앱, 소매점 재고 관리 앱) · 적용 레슨으로 STR-10-02, STR-10-03, STR-10-05 개념을 사용
insight: 앱은 코드만 국경을 공짜로 넘는다. 어디로, 무엇을 바꿔, 누구와 싸울지는 시장 사이의 거리와 현지 경쟁자가 정한다.
misconception: 앱은 번역하고 앱스토어에 올리면 어느 나라에서든 같은 방식으로 통한다.

sources.text: Ghemawat, P. (2001). Distance Still Matters: The Hard Reality of Global Expansion. Harvard Business Review. (시장 간 거리의 문화·제도·지리·경제 네 가지 구분의 배경)
모든 사례와 설정은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 사례(청소 예약 앱, 두 후보 국가, 재고 관리 앱, 현지 경쟁사)는 가상입니다. 국가 규모 비교(인구 1/3, 5배)는 설명용 설정이며 실제 국가를 가리키지 않습니다.
3번 카드의 '네 가지 거리' 구분은 Ghemawat(2001)의 틀을 쉬운 말로 옮긴 것입니다. 프레임워크 이름은 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다. STR-10-02 개념 레슨의 용어와 일치하는지 확인하세요.
청소 인력 고용·지급 방식이 나라마다 다르다는 내용은 일반적 서술로만 두었고, 특정 국가의 노동법 조언은 하지 않습니다.

cards.title: Your app can launch anywhere. Your business can't.
body: A home-cleaning booking app is thriving in its home city. Customers book in two taps, cleaners get steady work, and reviews are strong.
Going abroad looks easy: translate the screens, list the app in another country's store. But the code is the only part that travels for free.

image.label: A phone with a cleaning app, a world map behind it
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 스마트폰 화면에 청소 예약 앱(빗자루 아이콘, 예약 버튼). 뒤에 지도가 있고 폰에서 다른 나라로 점선이 뻗어 나가는데, 점선 중간에 작은 장애물(말풍선, 동전, 시계, 서류)이 놓여 있음. 실제 앱 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which country first?
body: The founder has two options. **Country A** is next door: a similar language, the same card-payment habits, but a third of the population.
**Country B** is far away and five times bigger. There, most households hire cleaners by word of mouth and pay in cash.

options.text: Country B. The bigger market pays for the extra effort
options.feedback: Size is real, but so is distance. Different language, payment habits and hiring customs each add cost, and together they can swallow the bigger market's advantage.

options.text: Country A. A closer market is cheaper to win
options.feedback: This is **the distance between markets** at work: a small market close to you can be worth more than a big one far away. You learn faster and cheaper, and B can come later.

options.text: Both at once, to beat rivals to each
options.feedback: Speed matters if rivals are close. But two launches split a small team, and you won't know which problems come from the app and which from the country.

cards.title: Distance isn't only kilometres.
body: Country B looked far for four kinds of reasons. Only one shows up on a map.
list: **Culture:** letting a stranger into your home is about trust, and trust is built differently in each place
**Rules:** how cleaners can be hired and paid differs by country
**Geography:** a cleaning app needs cleaners in every city it serves; you can't send them from home
**Money:** local wages and prices change what a booking is worth
cards.callout: An app shrinks some distances. It rarely removes them.
cards.softwareNote: Look at your own product: what a customer touches before paying is where distance shows up first.

cards.title: You launched next door. What do you change?
body: Country A it is. Early customers like the app, but bookings grow slowly. Where do you spend your next three months?

options.text: Finish the translation and keep everything else the same
options.feedback: Cheapest to run, but it treats the market as identical. Small differences in how people pay and choose cleaners can quietly stall growth.

options.text: Keep booking and reviews as they are; adapt payments, cleaner checks and prices
options.feedback: This is **localize or standardize** at work. Keep the parts customers don't notice the same, so you run one product. Adapt the parts that decide trust and price.

options.text: Rebuild the app around local tastes, with a new name and design
options.feedback: It may feel local, but now you run two products. Every future feature costs double, and you throw away what already works.

cards.title: Keep the engine. Adapt the handshake.
body: In most apps the engine is invisible: search, scheduling, booking, reviews. Customers don't care whether it matches the version in another country.
The handshake is what they touch when deciding to trust you: how they pay, who vouches for the worker, how the price looks, which language support speaks.
Keep the engine the same everywhere. Adapt the handshake to each market.

image.label: An engine block labeled 'same' and a handshake labeled 'local'
image.brief: 좌우 2분할 인포그래픽. 왼쪽은 회색 톱니바퀴 엔진에 "Same everywhere: search, booking, reviews" 라벨. 오른쪽은 두 손이 악수하는 그림에 "Local: payment, trust checks, price, language" 라벨. 오른쪽에 나라별로 색이 다른 작은 손 3개.

cards.title: Every local change is a product you maintain.
body: Adapting to a market often shows respect for customers. But each local payment method, rule and price list needs testing, support and updates, for as long as you stay.
A team that adapts everything in three countries can end up running three companies. Before each change, ask one question: will customers notice if we don't?

cards.title: Now it's a stock app for small shops.
body: Your app helps corner shops track stock and reorder from suppliers. In your new country, one local company already serves most shops.
Its app is plainer than yours, but it connects to the two biggest local wholesalers, where shops buy most of their goods.

options.text: Cut your price in half to pull shops away
options.feedback: The **local champion** knows the market and can match your price. A price war spends your money exactly where it is strongest.

options.text: Launch with better features and let shops compare
options.feedback: Better features help, but shops chose the rival for its wholesaler links, not its screens. Without those links, your edge may not count.

options.text: Partner with a mid-sized wholesaler the rival doesn't connect to, and start with its shops
options.feedback: This respects the **local champion**'s real strength, its local ties, instead of attacking it head on. You build local ties of your own and win one corner first.

cards.title: Going abroad is a strategy question, not a translation job.
body: This lesson used three ideas from the unit: **the distance between markets** to choose where to go, **localize or standardize** to choose what to change, and **local champions** to choose how to compete.
**Try it today:** pick one market you'd like to enter. Write one difference each in culture, rules, geography and money. Which one would hurt most?
